sections.section_title: Case Presentation and Initial Clinical Assessment
sections.description: This section introduces the patient's presentation to the emergency department, including relevant medical history, the sequence of events leading to anaphylaxis, vital signs, physical examination findings, and the immediate clinical recognition of anaphylaxis as a diagnosis.
subtopics: Patient demographics, medical history, and known drug allergies
Timeline of antibiotic exposure: from clindamycin rash to clarithromycin-induced anaphylaxis
Presenting symptoms: pruritus, flushing, throat swelling sensation, agitation
Initial vital signs demonstrating hypotension and hypoxemia
Physical examination findings: facial swelling, generalized erythema, and urticaria
Clinical criteria for diagnosing anaphylaxis in the emergency setting

sections.section_title: Pathophysiology of Anaphylaxis and Definitions of Complex Courses
sections.description: This section provides the foundational knowledge needed to understand anaphylaxis, its pathophysiological mechanisms, and the definitions of biphasic and multiphasic reactions that distinguish this case from typical presentations.
subtopics: IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation and release of inflammatory mediators
Clinical diagnostic criteria for anaphylaxis involving multiple organ systems
Definition and pathophysiology of biphasic anaphylaxis
Definition of multiphasic anaphylaxis and differentiation from refractory anaphylaxis
Epidemiology of biphasic reactions: reported incidence and timing of recurrence
Challenges in identifying true biphasic reactions versus ongoing allergen absorption

sections.section_title: Acute Management and the Challenge of Recurrent Episodes
sections.description: This section details the management approach for this patient's multiple anaphylactic episodes, including epinephrine administration, adjunctive therapies, ICU admission decisions, and the clinical reasoning behind treatment modifications.
subtopics: First-line treatment: intramuscular epinephrine administration and dosing considerations
Epinephrine auto-injector dosing (0.3 mg) versus recommended adult dosing (0.5 mg)
Management of four distinct anaphylactic episodes with progressively decreasing severity
Adjunctive therapies: antihistamines, intravenous fluids, and supplemental oxygen
Corticosteroid administration and the rationale despite evolving evidence against routine use
ICU admission for enhanced monitoring after first relapse
Allergology consultation and consideration of alternative treatment strategies

sections.section_title: Diagnostic Evaluation for Underlying Mast Cell Disorders
sections.description: This section explores the investigation into why this patient experienced an atypical multiphasic course, focusing on tryptase measurement, the workup for systemic mastocytosis, and how the findings inform our understanding of her condition.
subtopics: Tryptase measurement: recommended timing intervals and clinical utility
Interpretation of elevated tryptase levels during and after anaphylaxis
Systemic mastocytosis: pathophysiology and association with severe anaphylaxis
WHO diagnostic criteria for systemic mastocytosis (major and minor criteria)
Findings consistent with systemic mastocytosis: elevated baseline tryptase, hepatomegaly, neuropsychiatric symptoms
Why formal diagnostic criteria were not met: limitations of bone marrow biopsy

sections.section_title: Clinical Outcome, Discharge Planning, and Long-term Management
sections.description: This section covers the patient's resolution of symptoms, transition from ICU to ward care, discharge planning including medication and education, and the importance of follow-up in patients with complex anaphylaxis.
subtopics: Resolution of symptoms after 24 hours without recurrence
Hospital course and total length of admission
Discharge medications: levocetirizine and epinephrine auto-injector
Patient education on anaphylaxis recognition and auto-injector use
Allergy avoidance strategies and decision against confirmatory skin testing
Long-term allergology follow-up and monitoring of tryptase levels

sections.description: This section synthesizes current evidence on anaphylaxis management, highlights important clinical lessons from this case, and addresses knowledge gaps that affect the care of patients with biphasic or multiphasic anaphylaxis.
subtopics: Current evidence on corticosteroids: systematic reviews showing lack of benefit in preventing biphasic reactions
Epinephrine dosing concerns: underdosing with 0.3 mg auto-injectors in adults over 50 kg
Observation protocols: risk stratification approaches and optimal monitoring duration
Systemic mastocytosis as a predisposing factor for severe and complex anaphylaxis
Identified predictors of biphasic anaphylaxis and their clinical limitations
Knowledge gaps in multiphasic anaphylaxis management and the need for case registries
